è uno strategico a turni veramente ben fatto, apparentemente semplice nella gestione, ma è invece molto complesso nella parte strategica vera e propria, e il bello è che questo rispecchia proprio il tipo di guerra che vuole rappresentare, ovvero quella contro un nemico non visibile, che utilizza la guerriglia nella sua essenza, come unica forma di scontro (imboscate, linee di rifornimento difficili da scoprire, attacchi fulminei ed ritirate altrettanto rapide, postazioni contraeree improvvisate ma molto efficienti perché nascoste nella giungla, etc etc). Non potrete pianificare battaglie campali, come nei classici strategici, qui ogni mossa va calcolata tenendo conto anche dell'imprevedibilità del nemico, che tuttavia non è casuale (anche il nemico ha delle basi e delle linee di rifornimento). Anche la parte forse più snervante, come rifornire continuamente via elicottero i plotoni in esplorazione lontani dalle basi, o recuperare i feriti, col rischio pure che gli elicotteri vengano abbattuti, ricrea perfettamente quelle situazioni tipiche e uniche della guerra in Vietnam. Non c'è una campagna con missioni consequenziali, ma solo delle mappe skirmish generate di volta in volta con la possibilità di variare alcuni parametri. Forse la presenza di una "storia" o di missioni con "obiettivi" avrebbe reso più accattivante lo spirito del gioco. Tuttavia ogni partita vive a sé, e ti poni tu stesso gli obiettivi per arrivare al turno finale con l'influenza sulla regione maggiore del 50% necessaria per vincere. Anche in questo senso è fedele a quella guerra, non essendo stata una guerra di conquista o di rivendicazione di territori.

A solid wargame set in the relatively rare Vietnam War setting.  

The player commands regular units of the US and South Vietnamese armies, facing off against the Viet Cong and the regular forces of the North Vietnamese Army. I can’t say how accurately the developers managed to recreate the realities of guerrilla warfare, but it felt quite realistic to me, even if somewhat simplified.  

The US Army is stronger but far smaller in numbers. The Viet Cong is highly mobile, constantly appearing behind your lines, laying mines on roads and fields, intimidating civilians, and setting ambushes, though they are quite weak in open combat. The North Vietnamese Army is stronger but less mobile and operates more traditionally by establishing bases and attacking the player’s bases and units, sometimes with heavy equipment.  

Most of the player’s time is spent organizing supply lines and gathering intelligence.  

The game is well-suited for newcomers to the genre: it’s not overly complex, there aren’t too many units to manage, and a single session lasts about an hour to an hour and a half. For seasoned veterans of the genre, it might feel overly simplistic.

It is amazing when you find a game that seems it was made just for you. I have often dreamed of a strategy game that focused on the softer parts of war, hearts and minds and politics and logistics, rather than the obsessive focus games have on violence and destruction. Vietnam is a great example where the US won the battles but still lost the war. This game gives you the opportunity to see that in action and succeed where the US failed. Few games that can portray COIN operations in a realistic fashion. This game succeeds and I think it draws an excellent line when it comes to complexity vs accessibility. It is a matter of focusing on logistics and intelligence to support regional security and win hearts and minds of the populace (while balancing politics at home). Some may disagree, saying the game is far too simplistic and once you figure it out lacks enough depth to keep you interested long-term. Fair enough, this game is much like a puzzle at first. Once you figure it out, the custom settings offer some replayability. You can complete your uniform for achievements. But, that may be about all that'll hold your attention. But, for the price you pay, you'll get a lot of mileage out of this excellent, well designed game. I have played this game offline a lot (which is why my hours are low). But, I'd estimate I've put at least 30-40 hours into it and still come back to it from time to time to play a campaign. The developer has made a sequel with greater depth, Afghanistan '11. And Angola '86 is on its way. But I recommend starting with this game. It is a great introduction to this unique 'series'.

Vietnam '65 is really closer to the design of a great board game than to that of a traditional PC wargame. It's a single scenario that works according to very specific rules. But it also stands up to repeated play. I feel like it has its limits, even on Veteran difficulty, because there are places where you can exploit the system. A few Green Beret recon units running around in the jungle can usually find juicy targets every turn or so, and at that point I'm essentially harvesting Viet Cong units for points, and that starts to make things run a little too smoothly and predictably for a game about Vietnam.
One small but annoying problem is the game's dual identity as a tablet and PC wargame. The UI probably makes a lot of sense on a tablet, but it wastes the right mouse button, and the radial command menu gets in the way of the parts of the map you want to see. Even after many hours with the game, I have a few too many misclicks in each game.
Still, how many games about Vietnam have even come close to doing the subject justice? Heck, how many games make loading and unloading troop transports into something fun? On the PC, I can't name a single current game that has dealt with this subject and accomplished its goals so well.

Vietnam '65 is all about three things; intelligence, logistics, and winning over the hearts and minds of the people you're supposed to be helping.

Intelligence is key; you can't bring your awesome firepower to bear if you can't find the enemy. Improper scouting leaves your units open to ambush. Careless flying over the jungle could result in a helicopter shot down. If you're not actively seeking out the enemy, they'll lay mines around villages and set up ready to ambush.

How proficient you become at managing logistics determines how far you can reach out across the map. All units need periodic resupply, even the helicopters ferrying supplies. Overstretch yourself and you're in trouble. Vehicles can only be refuelled by engineers, so you need to keep them nearby to keep your tanks and APC's rolling. Helicopters also handle medevac so they're an absolutely critical part of your operation -- just like the real war.

Winning over the hearts and minds involves finding and eliminating the enemy, clearing minefields, and not taking heavy casualties. Sweeping mines and destroying the enemy will endear a nearby village to you, but if a helicopter is shot down nearby they'll lose faith. You've got to actually defend these people and be proactive to keep them on your side.

It's not a hugely long game, and replayability comes down to how excited you are to play again, but for the price I was happy and I'll be playing it through again some time in the future. It's just the right length, imo, for what it's going for.

I wish there was.. something for when you've won a campaign. Some kind of score screen, outro movie, text scroll? It just displays a victory screen and kicks back to the menu. It's fine, it's not a massive thing, it's just a bit of polish that would've really helped.

I also wish it was LMB to select/deselect and then RMB to give orders, rather than all being on LMB with RMB as deselect. I gave far too many bogus orders when I meant to select a unit. It's a problem strategy games solved a long time ago so I'm perplexed why this game recreates that old issue?

Anyway, cool interesting and unique strategy game, big thumbs up.

This is a tactical game with a small element of hearts and minds. The physical and time scales are unclear. My guess is that a hex is about 2km across and a turn maybe half a day. This does raise questions about the choppers which fly for 4 or 5 turns before refuelling...
The game is mainly about detecting and then destroying VC and NVA units. You can recruit a variety of US and ARVN units to help achieve this goal. Your ultimate aim is to have a network of units enabling you to monitor activity across most of the board, and then some mobile units to respond to identified threats. Your only PSYOPS options are to visit villages periodically, most of the hearts and minds score comes from killing enemy units.
The game works OK but has a lot of micromanagement - you have to keep resupplying units, so you spend a lot of time sending choppers out and back. Miscounting by a hex can mean a chopper crashes due to running out of fuel - the lack of an undo, or range warning hurts a bit here.
In game play terms, my main issue is that there is very strong positive feedback - win the first few fights and you'll likely win the game, as you will have earned money to buy reinforcements, upgraded your units, gained intelligence, and boosted your score. Conversely lose the first few fights and you have lost money, gained no intel, and in fact decreased your odds of getting further intel. Given that the early fights tend to be around 50/50, this positive feedback feels a bit too strong. 
Not sure about replayability - the board differs a bit, but the real decisions are around recruitment choices, and I can't see that varying much. Overall good but not great.

Pros: turn-based strategy. I love the genre. There aren't enough tbs games out there, and even fewer good ones. This one is borderline at best. Its challenging, though mainly because of manufactured difficulty. Interesting model of guerilla warfare where enemies attack you and melt back into the jungle, whether they win or lose the skirmish. Frustrating as hell!

Cons: Simplistic to the extreme. There's absolutely no overwatch for your units, though the enemy seems to be able to enjoy it on occasion. Enemy units can attack you with impunity while they're standing right next to your base with artillery in it; zero fire support. But you attack their base, and they're pelting you with shells as soon as you're two hexes away. Enemy units appear out of thin air, despite the game claiming they spawn "on the Ho Chi Min Trail". Line of sight is practically non-existent. Only two units can see past their own hex; Green Berets can two hexes beyond, and regular infantry can see one beyond. Air units are blind whether on open ground or over the jungle canopy. The enemy has RPGs. You have nothing but rifles. No bazookas, no M79s, nothing to counter this powerful tool. Like I said... manufactured difficulty.

Still, I'll recommend it if you don't mind getting stressed out over a mobile quality game that could have been so much more than a half-assed money grab.
